Shared Domains: Network optimization for multicast IPTV delivery, client-server assignment, and quality-of-experience performance.
GPU-accelerated graph algorithms and data structures for combinatorial counting problems.
Multi-core processing efficiency prediction using CPU and memory resource modeling.
Algorithmic complexity, approximation heuristics, and empirical performance evaluation.
Method-Application Synergies: Mixed-integer programming client-assignment models were applied to multicast IPTV networks to minimize zap time and bandwidth.
GPU CUDA memory-hierarchy techniques were applied to graph counting problems such as subgraphs, cliques, and independent sets.
Composite CPU and memory prediction models were applied to multi-core task scheduling and distributed-systems load balancing.
Complementary Technique Synergies: NP-hard client assignment models were paired with polynomial-time heuristics for a relaxed problem.
BFS-tree graph splitting and balanced upper-triangular adjacency storage were paired with GPU CUDA multithreading.
Analytical upper/lower efficiency bounds were paired with empirical UNIX benchmark experiments and statistical analysis.
Data-Method Synergies: Random IPTV server-tree and client channel-request instances were analyzed using Gurobi mixed-integer optimization.
Graphs stored in GPU shared and global memory were analyzed using adjacency, upper-triangular, and BFS-tree structures.
UNIX benchmark programs parameterized by CPU usage and memory requirement were used to validate efficiency models.
Cross-Domain Fusion Topics: IPTV quality-of-experience optimization through NP-hard multicast client assignment over constrained trees.
Memory-efficient GPU graph storage enabling combinatorial counting of subgraphs, cliques, and independent sets.
Composite CPU-memory modeling connecting analytical resource-availability bounds with multi-core execution efficiency.
Shared Application Areas: IPTV network operation, channel-change performance, and multicast bandwidth conservation.
Graph analytics for social networks, web graphs, and biological systems.
Distributed-systems scheduling, load balancing, and multi-core resource management.
Joint Technique Development: Client Assignment Problem variants MB, MZ, MZCB, and MBCZ with relaxed heuristics BZ, BZP, and GRC.
BFS-tree-based graph splitting and balanced upper-triangular adjacency storage for GPU shared memory.
Composite execution-efficiency bounds and a CPU availability average prediction model for multi-core workloads.
Theory-Application Synergy: NP-hardness reduction from minimum set cover justified heuristic design for IPTV client assignment.
BFS-tree properties and GPU memory-hierarchy constraints informed parallel graph counting speedups.
CPU availability and memory-paging theory informed empirical multi-core efficiency prediction.
Thinking Pattern Synergies: Formal optimization and complexity analysis were reinforced by generated network-instance experiments.
Memory-constrained data-structure design was reinforced by GPU hardware performance measurements.
Theoretical bounds were reinforced by benchmark-based statistical validation of prediction accuracy.
Future Research Directions: Scaling IPTV client assignment using relaxed heuristics as initial states for integer optimization.
Improving GPU graph counting for larger graphs stored in global memory.
Extending composite CPU-memory efficiency prediction to dynamic workloads and distributed scheduling decisions.
Summary Collaboration Themes: The collaboration centers on performance-driven computing and systems optimization. In IPTV work, the researchers formalized client-to-server assignment as NP-hard integer programs, balancing zap time and multicast bandwidth, then derived relaxed polynomial-time heuristics and evaluated them empirically. In GPU graph work, they designed memory-efficient graph representations and BFS-based partitioning to accelerate counting subgraphs, cliques, and independent sets. In multi-core modeling, they combined CPU availability and memory requirements into composite analytical bounds, validated with UNIX benchmarks. Together, these publications show a consistent pattern: formulate system constraints, develop analytical or algorithmic tools, and validate on realistic or empirical workloads.
